caseStudies.name: Contoso, Ltd.
caseStudies.text:
HOTSPOT
-
Case study
-
This is a case study. Case studies are not timed separately. You can use as much exam time as you would like to complete each case. However,
there may be additional case studies and sections on this exam. You must manage your time to ensure that you are able to complete all questions
included on this exam in the time provided.
To answer the questions included in a case study, you will need to reference information that is provided in the case study. Case studies might
contain exhibits and other resources that provide more information about the scenario that is described in the case study. Each question is
independent of the other questions in this case study.
At the end of this case study, a review screen will appear. This screen allows you to review your answers and to make changes before you move to
the next section of the exam. After you begin a new section, you cannot return to this section.
To start the case study
-
To display the first question in this case study, click the Next button. Use the buttons in the left pane to explore the content of the case study
before you answer the questions. Clicking these buttons displays information such as business requirements, existing environment, and problem
statements. If the case study has an All Information tab, note that the information displayed is identical to the information displayed on the
subsequent tabs. When you are ready to answer a question, click the Question button to return to the question.
Overview
-
Contoso, Ltd. is a US-based health supplements company. Contoso has two divisions named Sales and Research. The Sales division contains two
departments named Online Sales and Retail Sales. The Research division assigns internally developed product lines to individual teams of
researchers and analysts.
Existing Environment
-
Identity Environment
-
Contoso has a Microsoft Entra tenant named contoso.com. The tenant contains two groups named ResearchReviewersGroup1 and
ResearchReviewersGroup2.
Data Environment
-
Contoso has the following data environment:
• The Sales division uses a Microsoft Power BI Premium capacity.
• The semantic model of the Online Sales department includes a fact table named Orders that uses Import made. In the system of origin, the
OrderID value represents the sequence in which orders are created.
• The Research department uses an on-premises, third-party data warehousing product.
• Fabric is enabled for contoso.com.
• An Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 storage account named storage1 contains Research division data for a product line named Productline1. The
data is in the delta format.
• A Data Lake Storage Gen2 storage account named storage2 contains Research division data for a product line named Productline2. The data is
in the CSV format.
Requirements
-
Planned Changes
-
Contoso plans to make the following changes:
• Enable support for Fabric in the Power BI Premium capacity used by the Sales division.
• Make all the data for the Sales division and the Research division available in Fabric.
• For the Research division, create two Fabric workspaces named Productline1ws and Productline2ws.
• In Productline1ws, create a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.
• In Lakehouse1, create a shortcut to storage1 named ResearchProduct.
Data Analytics Requirements
-
Contoso identifies the following data analytics requirements:
• All the workspaces for the Sales division and the Research division must support all Fabric experiences.
• The Research division workspaces must use a dedicated, on-demand capacity that has per-minute billing.
• The Research division workspaces must be grouped together logically to support OneLake data hub filtering based on the department name.
• For the Research division workspaces, the members of ResearchReviewersGroup1 must be able to read lakehouse and warehouse data and
shortcuts by using SQL endpoints.
• For the Research division workspaces, the members of ResearchReviewersGroup2 must be able to read lakehouse data by using Lakehouse
explorer.
• All the semantic models and reports for the Research division must use version control that supports branching.
Data Preparation Requirements
-
Contoso identifies the following data preparation requirements:
• The Research division data for Productline1 must be retrieved from Lakehouse1 by using Fabric notebooks.
• All the Research division data in the lakehouses must be presented as managed tables in Lakehouse explorer.
Semantic Model Requirements
-
Contoso identifies the following requirements for implementing and managing semantic models:
• The number of rows added to the Orders table during refreshes must be minimized.
• The semantic models in the Research division workspaces must use Direct Lake mode.
General Requirements
-
Contoso identifies the following high-level requirements that must be considered for all solutions:
• Follow the principle of least privilege when applicable.
• Minimize implementation and maintenance effort when possible.

caseStudies.text:
HOTSPOT
-
Case study
-
This is a case study. Case studies are not timed separately. You can use as much exam time as you would like to complete each case. However,
there may be additional case studies and sections on this exam. You must manage your time to ensure that you are able to complete all questions
included on this exam in the time provided.
To answer the questions included in a case study, you will need to reference information that is provided in the case study. Case studies might
contain exhibits and other resources that provide more information about the scenario that is described in the case study. Each question is
independent of the other questions in this case study.
At the end of this case study, a review screen will appear. This screen allows you to review your answers and to make changes before you move to
the next section of the exam. After you begin a new section, you cannot return to this section.
To start the case study
-
To display the first question in this case study, click the Next button. Use the buttons in the left pane to explore the content of the case study
before you answer the questions. Clicking these buttons displays information such as business requirements, existing environment, and problem
statements. If the case study has an All Information tab, note that the information displayed is identical to the information displayed on the
subsequent tabs. When you are ready to answer a question, click the Question button to return to the question.
Overview
-
Litware, Inc. is a manufacturing company that has offices throughout North America. The analytics team at Litware contains data engineers,
analytics engineers, data analysts, and data scientists.
Existing Environment
-
Fabric Environment
-
Litware has been using a Microsoft Power BI tenant for three years. Litware has NOT enabled any Fabric capacities and features.
Available Data
-
Litware has data that must be analyzed as shown in the following table.
The Product data contains a single table and the following columns.
The customer satisfaction data contains the following tables:
• Survey
• Question
• Response
For each survey submitted, the following occurs:
• One row is added to the Survey table.
• One row is added to the Response table for each question in the survey.
The Question table contains the text of each survey question. The third question in each survey response is an overall satisfaction score.
Customers can submit a survey after each purchase.
User Problems
-
The analytics team has large volumes of data, some of which is semi-structured. The team wants to use Fabric to create a new data store.

Product data is often classified into three pricing groups: high, medium, and low. This logic is implemented in several databases and semantic
models, but the logic does NOT always match across implementations.
Requirements
-
Planned Changes
-
Litware plans to enable Fabric features in the existing tenant. The analytics team will create a new data store as a proof of concept (PoC). The
remaining Liware users will only get access to the Fabric features once the PoC is complete. The PoC will be completed by using a Fabric trial
capacity
The following three workspaces will be created:
• AnalyticsPOC: Will contain the data store, semantic models, reports pipelines, dataflow, and notebooks used to populate the data store
• DataEngPOC: Will contain all the pipelines, dataflows, and notebooks used to populate OneLake
• DataSciPOC: Will contain all the notebooks and reports created by the data scientists
The following will be created in the AnalyticsPOC workspace:
• A data store (type to be decided)
• A custom semantic model
• A default semantic model
• Interactive reports
The data engineers will create data pipelines to load data to OneLake either hourly or daily depending on the data source. The analytics engineers
will create processes to ingest, transform, and load the data to the data store in the AnalyticsPOC workspace daily. Whenever possible, the data
engineers will use low-code tools for data ingestion. The choice of which data cleansing and transformation tools to use will be at the data
engineers’ discretion.
All the semantic models and reports in the Analytics POC workspace will use the data store as the sole data source.
Technical Requirements
-
The data store must support the following:
• Read access by using T-SQL or Python
• Semi-structured and unstructured data
• Row-level security (RLS) for users executing T-SQL queries
Files loaded by the data engineers to OneLake will be stored in the Parquet format and will meet Delta Lake specifications.
Data will be loaded without transformation in one area of the AnalyticsPOC data store. The data will then be cleansed, merged, and transformed
into a dimensional model
The data load process must ensure that the raw and cleansed data is updated completely before populating the dimensional model
The dimensional model must contain a date dimension. There is no existing data source for the date dimension. The Litware fiscal year matches
the calendar year. The date dimension must always contain dates from 2010 through the end of the current year.

The product pricing group logic must be maintained by the analytics engineers in a single location. The pricing group data must be made available
in the data store for T-SOL. queries and in the default semantic model. The following logic must be used:
• List prices that are less than or equal to 50 are in the low pricing group.
• List prices that are greater than 50 and less than or equal to 1,000 are in the medium pricing group.
• List prices that are greater than 1,000 are in the high pricing group.
Security Requirements
-
Only Fabric administrators and the analytics team must be able to see the Fabric items created as part of the PoC.
Litware identifies the following security requirements for the Fabric items in the AnalyticsPOC workspace:
• Fabric administrators will be the workspace administrators.
• The data engineers must be able to read from and write to the data store. No access must be granted to datasets or reports.
• The analytics engineers must be able to read from, write to, and create schemas in the data store. They also must be able to create and share
semantic models with the data analysts and view and modify all reports in the workspace.
• The data scientists must be able to read from the data store, but not write to it. They will access the data by using a Spark notebook
• The data analysts must have read access to only the dimensional model objects in the data store. They also must have access to create Power
BI reports by using the semantic models created by the analytics engineers.
• The date dimension must be available to all users of the data store.
• The principle of least privilege must be followed.
Both the default and custom semantic models must include only tables or views from the dimensional model in the data store. Litware already
has the following Microsoft Entra security groups:
• FabricAdmins: Fabric administrators
• AnalyticsTeam: All the members of the analytics team
• DataAnalysts: The data analysts on the analytics team
• DataScientists: The data scientists on the analytics team
• DataEngineers: The data engineers on the analytics team
• AnalyticsEngineers: The analytics engineers on the analytics team
Report Requirements
-
The data analysts must create a customer satisfaction report that meets the following requirements:
• Enables a user to select a product to filter customer survey responses to only those who have purchased that product.
• Displays the average overall satisfaction score of all the surveys submitted during the last 12 months up to a selected dat.
• Shows data as soon as the data is updated in the data store.
• Ensures that the report and the semantic model only contain data from the current and previous year.
• Ensures that the report respects any table-level security specified in the source data store.
• Minimizes the execution time of report queries.

questions.stem:
You need to ensure that Contoso can use version control to meet the data analytics requirements and the general requirements.
What should you do?
questions.explanation:
The case study asks for *"version control that supports branching"* for the Research division semantic models and reports. Fabric **Git integration** is configured per workspace, under **Workspace settings → Git integration**, so the action is to point the **Research division workspaces** at a Git repository.

- **A / D** – Data Lake Gen2 and OneDrive are file stores. Neither gives you branches, merges or commit history, and neither is wired into Fabric's source-control experience.
- **B vs C** – when this question was written the doc said outright: *"Currently, only Git in Azure Repos with the same tenant as the Fabric tenant is supported."* That made **C** the only workable answer, and the community is 97% on C.

**Doc drift (worth knowing).** Microsoft added **GitHub** support in September 2024, so the current doc lists *both* Azure Repos and GitHub as supported providers. On today's docs B is no longer wrong on the technology — the remaining discriminator is wording: the requirement is scoped to the *Research division* workspaces (C), while B says "the Research workspaces". Pick **C**; it is right under both the old and the current documentation.

comments.body: "Currently, only Git in Azure Repos is supported." https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/cicd/git-integration/intro-to-git-integration?wt.mc_id=studentamb_657938#considerations-and-limitations

IMHO, the Azure Repos is the answer. It is directly mentioned here: https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/cicd/git-integration/intro-to-git-integration?wt.mc_id=studentamb_657938 Considerations and limitations Currently, only Git in Azure Repos with the same tenant as the Fabric tenant is supported. If the workspace and Git repo are in two different geographical regions, the tenant admin must enable cross-geo exports. Azure DevOps on-prem isn't supported. Sovereign clouds aren't supported.

https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/cicd/git-integration/intro-to-git-integration?tabs=azure-devops&wt.mc_id=studentamb_657938 Based on the Microsoft Learn new update dated 09/22/2024, both Git in Azure Repos(with the same tenant as the Fabric tenant) and GitHub is supported now. So the right answer for now are Azure Repos and GitHub.
B or C, but C is more specific for the division

Starting in September 2024, GitHub has also been supported for integration with Microsoft Fabric. At the time this question was created, the correct answer was only option C. Currently, both B and C are correct and support branching.
Now Github is also supported. What would be the correct answer now? Github or Azure Repos?
B. HitHub integration is now supported. (Preview) https://blog.fabric.microsoft.com/blog/announcing-github-integration-for-source-control-preview/?wt.mc_id=studentamb_657938
Microsoft copilot recommend option C:

questions.stem:
You need to recommend a solution to group the Research division workspaces.
What should you include in the recommendation? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**Domain — The Fabric Admin portal.**

The requirement is that *"the Research division workspaces must be grouped together logically to support OneLake data hub filtering based on the department name."* That is the textbook definition of a **domain**: *"a domain is a way of logically grouping together all the data in an organization that is relevant to a particular area or field."* Once workspaces are assigned to a domain, the OneLake data hub gains a domain filter — exactly the behaviour asked for.

- **Capacity** groups workspaces for *billing and compute*, not for data-hub filtering.
- **Tenant** is the whole organization; it is not a grouping you create.

Domains are created and managed by the Fabric admin (or a domain admin) in **Settings → Admin portal → Domains** — i.e. the **Fabric Admin portal**. The OneLake data hub is where you *consume* the resulting filter, not where you define the grouping, and the Microsoft Entra admin center manages identity, not Fabric content.

comments.body: Domain\Fabric Admin Portal

https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/governance/domains?wt.mc_id=studentamb_657938#create-a-domain From MS Learn 1. "In Fabric, a domain is a way to logically group together services in the organization" 2. You have to use Fabric Admin portal to do the groupings.

The right answer is Doamin \ OneLake Data Hub. The key wording is the Research Group will use 'Lakehouse Explorer'. This tool will connect to the Onelake Data Hub. From an admin perspective, you use the Fabric Admin portal to create the Domain Grouping. I think that is the confusion. Hope that helps someone.

Group method: Domain Tool: The Fabric Admin Portal The tool here should mean the tool to implement the grouping solution. Thus, the answer should be the Fabric admin portal instead. https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/governance/domains?wt.mc_id=studentamb_657938#create-a-domain
Should the tool not be Fabric Admin Portal? https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/governance/domains?wt.mc_id=studentamb_657938#configure-domain-settings
grouping is done via Data Hub not Fabric Admin Tool

IMHO, ** Domain / One Lake Data Hub ** Link: https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/governance/domains?wt.mc_id=studentamb_657938#create-a-domain 1. Because of this: In Fabric, a domain is a way of logically grouping together all the data in an organization that is relevant to a particular area or field. 2. Because of this: For instance, in the OneLake data hub, users can filter content by domain in order find content that is relevant to them. In addition, some tenant-level settings for managing and governing data can be delegated to the domain level, thus allowing domain-specific configuration of those settings.

But, if the question is how to do this, than answer may be Fabric Admin Portal, because of that: To assign workspaces to a domain or subdomain in the admin portal, you must be a Fabric admin or a domain admin. So, there is an ambiguity in a question

questions.stem:
You need to refresh the Orders table of the Online Sales department. The solution must meet the semantic model requirements.
What should you include in the solution?
questions.explanation:
The semantic model requirement is *"the number of rows added to the Orders table during refreshes must be minimized"*, and the case study tells you that **`OrderID` represents the sequence in which orders are created**. So an incremental load keyed on `OrderID` is the goal: read the **maximum** `OrderID` already in the destination, then pull only rows above it (a high-water-mark load).

- **Maximum, not minimum** – the minimum `OrderID` is the *oldest* order; filtering on it would re-load almost everything. That rules out **B** and **C**.
- **Dataflow, not stored procedure** – Microsoft documents this precise pattern as a dataflow tutorial: *"Set up incremental refresh with Dataflow Gen2"*, whose worked example adds a query that reads the maximum key from the data destination and filters the source against it. That leaves **D** over **A**.

refs.t: Set up incremental refresh with Dataflow Gen2

comments.body: we need to retrieve the maximum OrderID in the destination table to minimize the number of rows added during refresh. this would be an incremental load. can be done with data flows

D - As other people pointed out, the exact same use case for retrieving the max OrderID is showcased in the documentation https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-factory/tutorial-setup-incremental-refresh-with-dataflows-gen2?wt.mc_id=studentamb_657938#add-a-query-to-the-dataflow-to-filter-the-data-based-on-the-data-destination Thought at first that A would be correct because SP support least privilege and because how real incremental refresh is not yet supported in data flow gen 2 https://ideas.fabric.microsoft.com/ideas/idea/?ideaid=4814b098-efff-ed11-a81c-6045bdb98602
https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-factory/tutorial-setup-incremental-refresh-with-dataflows-gen2?wt.mc_id=studentamb_657938
Totally agree on the max value to be retrieved on incremental load

The Orders table uses Import mode, so minimizing the number of rows added during refreshes is crucial for performance and efficiency. By retrieving the maximum OrderID already present, you can incrementally load only new orders (i.e., those with OrderID > max). A Stored procedure activity is efficient and reusable for querying metadata like the max OrderID.
While option A, can also be considered. Option D is the best choice given that it requires minimal development and maintenance
key word minimize maintenance effort. answer is D

I'm also choosing D alongside the other answers. My reasoning is: 1) The showcased example of doing incremental refresh by dataflows (see the link below), which is almost an answer in itself because it tells you how Microsoft views the solution to this issue. 2) Maximum ID instead of minimum: see the same link for the specific use. But even without this knowledge you can read in the case study that new (higher) numbers represent newer orders, so for an incremental refresh it makes way more sense to retrieve the ID of the *latest* order placed than the ID of the first. 3) dataflow instead of stored procedure: because of the link, but it also makes sense from the "minimize implementation and maintenance effort" requirement: writing an incremental refresh SP is very, very complicated. Link: https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-factory/tutorial-setup-incremental-refresh-with-dataflows-gen2?wt.mc_id=studentamb_657938

r11CandidatePatch.stem: Candidate revision: a Fabric Data Factory pipeline incrementally appends strictly increasing, append-only OrderID values from a source into an explicitly maintained Orders destination table. No updates or late lower-ID arrivals occur. After reading the committed destination MAX(OrderID), which end-to-end process is appropriate?

options.text: Filter source OrderID greater than the committed maximum, append those rows, and update the checkpoint only after a successful load.
Load source rows below the minimum destination OrderID.
Append all source rows after every refresh without a checkpoint.
Read the maximum ID but do not filter or copy source rows.

r11CandidatePatch.explanation: Candidate adds the destination and append-only assumptions missing from the case. A maximum watermark must drive source filtering, loading and a successful checkpoint, not merely a query returning MAX. This variant is a pipeline exercise; it does not claim to repair Import semantic-model refresh by itself.

r11Review.reason: Designed a complete watermark task instead of treating MAX alone as a load.

optionReview.A: Proposed end-to-end append-only process.
optionReview.B: Wrong direction for monotonic new IDs.
optionReview.C: Reinserts existing rows.
optionReview.D: Does not perform a load.

adversarialReview.reviewer: Same model, separate counterargument pass; not an independent human or another agent
adversarialReview.challenge: This is a designed repair, not approval. Exact source fidelity, all final distractors, current feature scope and any necessary native execution remain open.

r11Review.remaining: Reconcile this derived pipeline variant with the original Import model requirement; verify pipeline activity and transaction/retry behavior before approval.
r11Review.approvalBasis: Documentation and explicitly stated scenario; no observed product execution

r10Finding.technical_conclusion: A high-water mark using the maximum OrderID is a defensible way to avoid inserting older rows for strictly ascending append-only source. However Contoso case only establishes Sales Orders as an imported semantic-model fact; it never establishes an Orders destination lakehouse or its ID column. Every choice refers to a destination lakehouse. A dataflow retrieving MAX on its own does not implement the required incremental load; the Fabric pipeline vs Azure Data Factory pipeline wording is also imprecise.
r10Finding.version_or_context_assumption: Contoso source case context exactly as supplied, without assuming an unstated data lakehouse in Sales.
correction_proposals: Specify concrete Orders lakehouse destination and its maintained last-inserted ID, or replace options with Import semantic model incremental refresh methods grounded in case.
Show filtering source OrderID greater than watermark, loading and checkpoint/update in an end-to-end data pipeline; document possible missing late arrivals/updates.
Name actual Azure Data Factory vs Fabric Data Factory feature explicitly.

option_by_option_analysis.A: MAX high-water mark appropriate, but stored procedure activity is not the tutorial solution for reading lakehouse destination; requires alternate SQL infrastructure
option_by_option_analysis.B: MIN would reprocess nearly all records; procedure path also differs
option_by_option_analysis.C: Dataflow is correct orchestration but MIN is wrong watermark
option_by_option_analysis.D: CORRECT: dataflow reads max destination OrderID and ingests > max

additional_independent_notes_R2.source_conclusion_reviewed: Option D implements a maximum-OrderID high-water mark with Dataflow Gen2, matching the documented incremental amass tutorial and case-study low maintenance requirement. It detects newly added orders only when OrderID advances; it does not capture corrections to earlier OrderIDs.

questions.stem: Which syntax should you use in a notebook to access the Research division data for Productline1?
questions.explanation:
The case study puts the shortcut **`ResearchProduct` inside `Lakehouse1`**, and requires that all Research division data *"be presented as managed tables in Lakehouse explorer"*. A shortcut created under the lakehouse's **Tables** area is surfaced as a table, so it can be queried by name with Spark SQL:

```python
df = spark.sql("SELECT * FROM Lakehouse1.ResearchProduct")
```

The OneLake shortcuts doc shows exactly these two forms side by side — `spark.read.format("delta").load("Tables/MyShortcut")` and `spark.sql("SELECT * FROM MyLakehouse.MyShortcut")`.

- **A** is the right *API* but the wrong *path*: the shortcut lives at `Tables/ResearchProduct`, not `Tables/productline1/ResearchProduct`. Productline1 is the workspace name, which is not part of the lakehouse's relative table path.
- **C / D** – `external_table(...)` is not a Fabric notebook construct at all (and C is missing a closing quote).

questions.stem:
You need to assign permissions for the data store in the AnalyticsPOC workspace. The solution must meet the security requirements.
Which additional permissions should you assign when you share the data store? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**Read All Apache Spark — Build Reports on the default dataset — Read All Apache Spark.**

These three checkboxes are the *additional* permissions offered when you share a lakehouse or warehouse. Sharing by itself already grants plain **Read** on the item; each extra box widens that. Match each one to the security requirement:

| Group | Requirement in the case study | Grant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **DataEngineers** | *"read from and write to the data store. **No access must be granted to datasets or reports**."* | **Read All Apache Spark** |
| **DataAnalysts** | *"create Power BI reports by using the semantic models created by the analytics engineers."* | **Build Reports on the default dataset** |
| **DataScientists** | *"read from the data store, but not write to it. **They will access the data by using a Spark notebook**."* | **Read All Apache Spark** |

- **DataEngineers** – the *"no access to datasets or reports"* clause eliminates *Build Reports on the default dataset* outright. Of the two remaining, Spark is the one that matches an engineer's read/write workload; the SQL analytics endpoint over a lakehouse is **read-only**, so it cannot satisfy "write to".
- **DataScientists** – the requirement names the access path explicitly ("by using a Spark notebook"), so it is *Read All Apache Spark*. This grant is read-only on its own, which also satisfies "but not write to it".

*Note:* the community splits on DataEngineers vs DataScientists (some swap Spark and SQL endpoint), but the two highest-voted comments (+91, +40) both land on Spark for the engineers, and the "Spark notebook" wording for the scientists is decisive.

questions.stem:
You need to create a DAX measure to calculate the average overall satisfaction score.
How should you complete the DAX code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**`AVERAGE('Survey'[Response Value]),` — `Period,`**

The measure is a rolling-12-month average, and the variables above the blanks do all the date work:

```dax
Rolling 12 Overall Satisfaction =
VAR NumberOfMonths = 12
VAR LastCurrentDate = MAX ( 'Date'[Date] )
VAR Period = DATESINPERIOD ( 'Date'[Date], LastCurrentDate, - NumberOfMonths, MONTH )
VAR Result =
  CALCULATE (
    <blank 1>
    <blank 2>
    'Survey Question'[Question Title] = "Overall Satisfaction"
  )
RETURN Result
```

**Blank 1 — the expression `CALCULATE` evaluates.** The satisfaction score is the numeric column `'Survey'[Response Value]`, so `AVERAGE('Survey'[Response Value])` is the whole calculation.
- `AVERAGEA('Question'[Question Text])` averages a *text* column. `AVERAGEA` coerces text to 0, so this returns 0 — meaningless here.
- `AVERAGEX(VALUES('Survey'[Customer Key]),` is syntactically incomplete as written (`AVERAGEX` needs a second `<expression>` argument), and averaging customer keys is not the ask.

**Blank 2 — the filter argument.** `CALCULATE` takes filters after the expression, and `Period` is already the `DATESINPERIOD(...)` table covering the last 12 months. Passing it filters the calculation to that window.
- `LastCurrentDate` is a single date (scalar), which would collapse the result to one day.
- `NumberOfMonths` is the integer 12 — not a filter at all.

questions.stem:
You need to resolve the issue with the pricing group classification.
How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**`VIEW` — `CASE` — `WHEN ListPrice BETWEEN 50 AND 1000) THEN 'medium'`.**

**The PDF's answer-key image is wrong on two of the three blanks** (it marks `TABLE` and `> 50 AND < 1000`). Here is the reasoning.

**Blank 1 — `VIEW`.** The requirement is *"The product pricing group logic must be maintained by the analytics engineers in a **single location**. The pricing group data must be made available in the data store for T-SQL queries **and in the default semantic model**."*
- A **view** stores the logic once and re-evaluates it on every read, so it can never drift from `dbo.Products` — that is what "single location" means. Views in a Fabric warehouse are queryable with T-SQL and are picked up by the default semantic model, which satisfies both halves of the requirement (the case study separately states that the semantic models *"must include only tables **or views** from the dimensional model"*).
- A **TABLE** (via CTAS) materialises a **copy**. The moment a list price changes, the copy is stale, and you now maintain the logic *and* a refresh job — the opposite of a single location.
- **FUNCTION** / **PROCEDURE** do not fit the `CREATE x [dbo].[ProductsWithPricingGroup] AS SELECT ...` shape shown, and a stored procedure is not exposed to the default semantic model.

**Blank 2 — `CASE`.** The block is `WHEN ... THEN ... END AS PricingGroup`, which is a searched `CASE` expression. `COALESCE` returns the first non-null argument, `IIF` takes exactly one condition, and `SET` is not an expression.

**Blank 3 — `BETWEEN`.** The spec is: low `<= 50`, medium `> 50 and <= 1000`, high `> 1000`. Check each option against **1,000**, the boundary that breaks two of them:

| Option | ListPrice = 1000 | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `> 50 AND < 1000` | no branch matches → **NULL** | wrong |
| `>= 50 AND < 1000` | no branch matches → **NULL** | wrong |
| `BETWEEN 50 AND 1000` | `BETWEEN` is inclusive → **'medium'** | correct |

`BETWEEN` also includes 50, which looks like an overlap with the low group — but it is not one, because **`CASE` evaluates its `WHEN` clauses in order and stops at the first match**. `ListPrice = 50` is caught by the preceding `WHEN ListPrice <= 50 THEN 'low'`, so it never reaches the `BETWEEN`. The documented behaviour: *"Evaluates, in the order specified, `Boolean_expression` for each `WHEN` clause … Returns `result_expression` of the first `Boolean_expression` that evaluates to TRUE."*

*Note:* the top comment (+77) makes exactly this argument. A second comment (+34) complains that all three options are wrong because none literally reads `> 50 AND <= 1000` — true, but it overlooks the short-circuit, which makes `BETWEEN` behave correctly. A third commenter who sat the exam reports Microsoft has since changed the live item to `WHEN(ListPrice > 50 AND ListPrice <= 1000)`; if you see that variant, pick it.

All options for the last one are wrong, which is irritating. Should be > 50 AND <= 1000.

I took the test the last week. This question was included, with a important modification: They changes the information,¡ of the first option for "WHEN": ListPrice > 50 AND ListPrice <= 1000) THEN 'medium'. -View -Case -WHEN(ListPrice > 50 AND ListPrice <= 1000) THEN 'medium'.

The range BETWEEN 50 AND 1000 is also a valid answer. However, if the value is 50, it will be returned from the previous ‘when’ clause, ListPrice <= 50 Then 'low', before reaching the second ‘when’ clause.”

I agree with your answer, but with some nuance: - I think that you're right that it is a view, but not because it is created from an existing table. Nothing prevents you from creating a table from a table (CTAS statement). However, it should be a view because 'data should be visible as soon as the datastore is updated'. A table from a table is not automatically refreshed when its source table is updated, but a view on this source table will immediately show the new results. - I agree that in the last option, there now is no correct option since none meet the requirements and BETWEEN is the least wrong. Either a bad question or a badly remembered question :)

* VIEW: from an existing table. * CASE: correct syntax before the WHENs. * WHEN(ListPrice > 50 AND ListPrice < 1000 THEN 'medium': The second option will generate 2 rows for any '50' answer; the third option has the same problem plus a miss spelled ' ) ' that will end up generating a syntax error. The only answer that will not generate a cartesian product is the first one, although it will miss all the '1000' answers.

The 3rd option is still the best--when doing a select with CASE WHEN, the logic is evaluated linearly. If the value is 50, the first case is true and the returned value is therefore "low". This can be tested with dummy data--just upload a csv file of numbers from 1 to 20 into a test warehouse and query in Fabric. select number, case when number <= 5 then 'low' when number between 5 and 10 then 'med' when number > 10 then 'high' end as test from dbo.numbers order by number asc As for the missing '(' or extra ')', I assume this is a typo.

questions.explanation:
The technical requirements for the AnalyticsPOC data store call for **"semi-structured and unstructured data"**, and state that files loaded to OneLake *"will be stored in the Parquet format and will meet Delta Lake specifications"*. questions.stem:
You have a Fabric warehouse that contains a table named Staging.Sales. Staging.Sales contains the following columns.
You need to write a T-SQL query that will return data for the year 2023 that displays ProductID and ProductName and has a summarized Amount
that is higher than 10,000.
Which query should you use?
A.
B.
C.
D.
questions.explanation:
Only **A** is valid T-SQL. The rule to apply is the logical order of evaluation: `FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY`. `WHERE` filters **rows** before grouping and cannot see aggregates; `HAVING` filters **groups** after aggregation and cannot see `SELECT` aliases.

```sql
SELECT ProductID, ProductName, SUM(Amount) AS TotalAmount
FROM Staging.Sales
WHERE DATEPART(YEAR, SaleDate) = '2023'   -- row filter, pre-aggregation
GROUP BY ProductID, ProductName
HAVING SUM(Amount) > 10000              -- group filter, repeats the aggregate
```

- **B** – puts the year test in `HAVING`, but `SaleDate` is neither in the `GROUP BY` list nor inside an aggregate, so it is not valid in a `HAVING` clause.
- **C** – uses `SUM(Amount)` inside `WHERE`. Aggregates are not allowed there (`WHERE` runs before grouping), and there is no `GROUP BY` to support the aggregate in the `SELECT` list either.
- **D** – references the alias `TotalAmount` in `HAVING`. `SELECT` aliases are only visible to `ORDER BY`; in `HAVING` you must repeat `SUM(Amount)`.

refs.t: Logical processing order of the SELECT statement

comments.body: Anything without HAVING() + an aggregate is incorrect. HAVING was created for SQL to deal with filtering using an aggregate. Any option that references TotalAmount is incorrect because there is no nested statement in the syntax. Anything that uses HAVING() + DATEPART() is incorrect because you use a where clause for that. The answer is A.
In D TotalAmount is an alias (HAVING TotalAmount > 10000) and only ORDER BY accepts aliases.
SELECT ProductID, ProductName, SUM(Amount) AS TotalAmount FROM Staging.Sales WHERE DATEPART(YEAR, SaleDate) = '2023' GROUP BY ProductID, ProductName HAVING SUM(Amount) > 10000
I would say Option D. Sum(Amount) AS TotalAmount is effectively TotalAmount > 10000
What was the point of having the Alias, if the Alias isn't being used in the Answer D. I realize everyone is saying A and yes that also would answer, but you can use the Column Alias also.

SELECT ProductID, ProductName, SUM(Amount) AS TotalAmount FROM Staging.Sales WHERE DATEPART(YEAR, SaleDate) = '2023' GROUP BY ProductID, ProductName HAVING SUM(Amount) > 10000 Answer A is the only answer with valid syntax. Answer B is excluded because the filter on year should be included in the WHERE-clause. It is the result of a function, but it is not an aggregate. Answer C is excluded because the filter on SUM(Amount) should be included in the HAVING-clause, since this is an aggregate. Answer D is excluded because the HAVING-clause does not accept aliases.

I am confused between A and B. But A is a correct Answer. Here is the explanation- If we use non-aggregate function to Having clause it will throw below error- Column 'SalesDate' is invalid in the HAVING clause because it is not contained in either an aggregate function or the GROUP BY clause.

In some instances, you might want to exclude individual rows from groups (using a WHERE clause) before applying a condition to groups as a whole (using a HAVING clause). A HAVING clause is like a WHERE clause, but applies only to groups as a whole (that is, to the rows in the result set representing groups), whereas the WHERE clause applies to individual rows. A query can contain both a WHERE clause and a HAVING clause. In that case: The WHERE clause is applied first to the individual rows in the tables or table-valued objects in the Diagram pane. Only the rows that meet the conditions in the WHERE clause are grouped. The HAVING clause is then applied to the rows in the result set. Only the groups that meet the HAVING conditions appear in the query output. You can apply a HAVING clause only to columns that also appear in the GROUP BY clause or in an aggregate function.

questions.stem:
You have a data warehouse that contains a table named Stage.Customers. Stage.Customers contains all the customer record updates from a
customer relationship management (CRM) system. There can be multiple updates per customer.
You need to write a T-SQL query that will return the customer ID, name. postal code, and the last updated time of the most recent row for each
customer ID.
How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**`ROW_NUMBER()` — `WHERE X = 1`.** This is the canonical "latest row per key" pattern: number the rows inside each customer, newest first, then keep number 1.

```sql
WITH CUSTOMERBASE AS (
  SELECT [CustomerID], [CustomerName], [PostalCode], [LastUpdated]
    , x = ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID ORDER BY LastUpdated DESC)
  FROM [LakehousePOC].[dbo].[CustomerChanges]
)
SELECT CustomerID, CustomerName, PostalCode, LastUpdated
FROM CUSTOMERBASE
WHERE X = 1;
```

**Blank 1.** `ROW_NUMBER()` *"numbers the output of a result set … starting at 1 for the first row in each partition."* With `ORDER BY LastUpdated DESC`, row 1 is the most recent update for that `CustomerID`.
- `LAST_VALUE()` returns a *value* from the window frame, not a rank, so there would be nothing to filter on — and by default its frame ends at the current row, a classic trap.
- `NTILE()` splits a partition into N buckets; it requires an argument and does not identify a single newest row.

**Blank 2.** Window functions cannot be referenced in `WHERE` in the same query level — that is precisely why the `ROW_NUMBER()` is computed in the CTE and filtered in the outer query. `WHERE X = 1` keeps the newest row per customer.
- `Having Max(LastUpdated) = 1` is nonsense: there is no `GROUP BY`, and comparing a datetime to 1 is a type error.
- `WHERE LastUpdated = Max(LastUpdated)` puts an aggregate in `WHERE`, which T-SQL rejects.

The PDF supplies only "Box 1: ROW_NUMBER()" with no key for box 2; the top comments (+39, +17, +5) all give the full query above.

Two other comments (+22, +12) answer **Yes**, and the PDF's answer-key image marks **Yes**. The wording is "a summary of the DataFrame", not "summary statistics", and the autogenerated report is exactly that — so Yes is the better reading.

Two facts decide every option here.

**1. The SQL analytics endpoint is read-only.** The doc states it plainly: *"The SQL analytics endpoint … is a read-only experience. You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse.
You use a dataflow to load a new dataset from OneLake to the warehouse.
You need to add a PowerQuery step to identify the maximum values for the numeric columns.
Which function should you include in the step?
questions.explanation:
Read the ask precisely: the maximum values for **the numeric columns** — plural, across columns, in **one** Power Query step.

**`Table.Profile`** does exactly that. It returns one row *per column* with the columns `Min`, `Max`, `Average`, `StandardDeviation`, `Count`, `NullCount` and `DistinctCount` — so a single step yields the maximum of every numeric column at once.

- **B `Table.Max`** returns *one row* — the largest row of the table according to a comparison criterion you must supply. It gives you a record, not a per-column maximum, and you would need a separate step per column.
- **A `Table.MaxN`** is the same idea for the *N* largest rows.
- **C `Table.Range`** returns a slice of rows by position. Nothing to do with maxima.

*Note:* about a third of the community votes B, arguing that "profiling" is a pane in the UI rather than a step. But `Table.Profile` is a genuine M function that you can add as a step, and it is the only option that answers the question for all numeric columns at once.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a machine learning model registered in a Fabric workspace.
You need to use the model to generate predictions by using the PREDICT function in a Fabric notebook.
Which two languages can you use to perform model scoring? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
The Fabric `PREDICT` function is a **Spark** construct. Microsoft documents three ways to call it, and the two that are offered here are **PySpark** and **Spark SQL**:

- the low-code **PREDICT wizard** in the ML model UI,
- the **Spark DataFrame API** from a notebook — `MLFlowTransformer(...)` in **PySpark** (and Scala/R),
- **Spark SQL**, by registering the model as a Spark SQL UDF and calling it in a `SELECT`.

- **A T-SQL** – Fabric notebooks do not run T-SQL, and `PREDICT` in a warehouse is a different, unrelated feature (it is not how you score a model registered in a Fabric workspace from a notebook).
- **B DAX** – a semantic-model query language. It has no model-scoring function and cannot run in a notebook.

The notebook language set is PySpark, Scala Spark, Spark SQL and SparkR — of the four options, only C and D are in it.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a Microsoft Power BI report named Report1. Report1 includes a Python visual.
Data displayed by the visual is grouped automatically and duplicate rows are NOT displayed.
You need all rows to appear in the visual.
What should you do?
questions.explanation:
Power BI aggregates the data it hands to a Python (or R) visual: identical rows are collapsed before the script ever runs. The documented workaround is to make every row distinguishable. From the *Tips* section of the Python visuals doc: *"In some cases, you might not want automatic grouping to occur, or you might want all rows to appear, including duplicates. In those cases, you can **add an index field to your dataset that causes all rows to be considered unique** and prevents grouping."*

Adding a field whose value is different on every row is exactly **C — add a unique field to each row**.

- **A** – *"Reference the columns in the Python code by index"* is about how your script addresses `dataset` columns. It changes nothing about the grouping Power BI has already applied before the script runs.
- **B** – *Sort Column By* controls display order only.
- **D** – *Summarize By* governs how a numeric column is aggregated in a visual (Sum, Average, …). Setting it to *Don't summarize* stops measures being summed, but the row-level de-duplication that feeds the Python visual still happens.

*Note:* the highest-voted comment (+73) answers **A** — but it quotes the doc sentence above, which describes adding an **index field** (a new column of unique values), not "referencing columns by index". A later comment (+13) catches the mix-up. The PDF key and 53% of the community are on **C**.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model. The model contains data about retail stores.
You need to write a DAX query that will be executed by using the XMLA endpoint. The query must return a table of stores that have opened since
December 1, 2023.
How should you complete the DAX expression? To answer, drag the appropriate values to the correct targets. Each value may be used once, more
than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**DEFINE — EVALUATE — SUMMARIZE.** A DAX *query* (the kind the XMLA endpoint executes, as opposed to a measure) has a fixed skeleton:

```dax
DEFINE
    VAR _SalesSince = DATE ( 2023, 12, 01 )
EVALUATE
    FILTER (
        SUMMARIZE ( Store, Store[Name], Store[OpenDate] ),
        Store[OpenDate] >= _SalesSince
    )
```

- **`DEFINE`** introduces the optional definition block. It is *"used to define entities that exist only for the duration of the query"* — here the `VAR _SalesSince`. It must come first, and a query may have at most one.
- **`EVALUATE`** is mandatory and introduces the table expression that the query returns: *"the EVALUATE statement … contains a table expression to be evaluated and returned."*
- **`SUMMARIZE`** is the missing function inside `FILTER`. `FILTER(<table>, <condition>)` needs a *table* as its first argument, and `SUMMARIZE(Store, Store[Name], Store[OpenDate])` produces the two-column table of stores that the filter then narrows to those opened on or after 1 December 2023.

- **`TABLE`** is not a DAX query keyword (it is a `DEFINE TABLE` sub-clause, which does not fit any of these slots).
- **`FILTER`** is already printed in the code, so it is a distractor in the Values pane.

You have a Fabric tenant that contains a workspace named Workspace1. Workspace1 is assigned to a Fabric capacity.
You need to recommend a solution to provide users with the ability to create and publish custom Direct Lake semantic models by using external
tools. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege.

questions.explanation:
Three things have to be true before a user can build and publish a custom Direct Lake model from an external tool such as Tabular Editor:

- **A — Tenant settings → *Allow XMLA Endpoints and Analyze in Excel with on-premises datasets* = Enabled.** This is the org-wide master switch for XMLA connectivity. With it off, nothing below matters.
- **D — Capacity settings → *XMLA Endpoint* = Read Write.** The capacity default is **Read Only**, which permits external tools to connect and query but not to deploy. Publishing a model requires **Read Write**.
- **E — Tenant settings → *Users can create Fabric items* = Enabled.** A Direct Lake semantic model is a Fabric item, so users need the right to create Fabric items at all.

Rejected:
- **B** *Allow Azure AD guest users…* – about external identities, irrelevant here, and granting it would violate least privilege.
- **C** *Users can edit data model in the Power BI service* – enables the **web** modelling experience. The requirement is **external tools** over XMLA, which is a different path.
- **F** *Publish to Web* – publishes reports anonymously to the public internet. Unrelated, and a serious least-privilege violation.

You are creating a semantic model in Microsoft Power BI Desktop.
You plan to make bulk changes to the model by using the Tabular Model Definition Language (TMDL) extension for Microsoft Visual Studio Code.

questions.explanation:
**PBIP — Power BI Project.** Saving as a project writes the report and the semantic model out as **plain-text folders on disk** instead of one binary file, which is what makes the model definition editable in VS Code and diffable in Git. The semantic model folder is where the **TMDL** files live (`definition/tables/*.tmdl`), so the TMDL extension for VS Code can open and bulk-edit them.

- **B PBIX** – the standard Power BI Desktop file. It is a single binary archive; external text tooling cannot edit the model inside it.
- **C PBIT** – a Power BI *template*: a PBIX without the data. Still binary, still not text-editable.
- **D PBIDS** – a tiny "data source" connection file used to start a new report against a given source. It contains no model at all.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1. Warehouse1 contains three schemas named schemaA, schemaB, and
schemaC.
You need to ensure that a user named User1 can truncate tables in schemaA only.
How should you complete the T-SQL statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**`GRANT ALTER ON SCHEMA::schemaA TO User1;`**

**The permission — `ALTER`.** There is no `TRUNCATE` permission in T-SQL. `TRUNCATE TABLE` requires, at minimum, **`ALTER` permission on the table**: *"The minimum permission required is ALTER on table_name."* Granting `ALTER` at the schema level covers every table in that schema, present and future.
- `CONNECT` only lets a principal open a connection to the database.
- `EXECUTE` applies to programmable objects (procedures, functions), not to truncating tables.

**The securable — `SCHEMA::schemaA`.** The requirement is *schemaA only*. Schema-scoped grants use the `SCHEMA::` class, and this scopes the permission to exactly one schema — schemaB and schemaC are untouched.
- `DATABASE::schemaA` is the wrong class *and* the wrong scope: it would name the whole database (and `schemaA` is not a database).
- `OBJECT::schemaA` scopes to a single object such as one table; `schemaA` is a schema, not an object.

*Note:* one commenter points out that Fabric Warehouse did not originally support `TRUNCATE TABLE`. That does not change the answer — the question is testing the GRANT syntax, and `ALTER ON SCHEMA::` is the least-privilege grant for it.

questions.stem:
You plan to deploy Microsoft Power BI items by using Fabric deployment pipelines. You have a deployment pipeline that contains three stages
named Development, Test, and Production. A workspace is assigned to each stage.
You need to provide Power BI developers with access to the pipeline. The solution must meet the following requirements:
Ensure that the developers can deploy items to the workspaces for Development and Test.
Prevent the developers from deploying items to the workspace for Production.
Follow the principle of least privilege.
Which three levels of access should you assign to the developers? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
Deployment pipelines need permission in **two** places: on the **pipeline** (to see and operate it) and on each **workspace** (to read from the source and write to the target). Least privilege then decides the level in each workspace.

- **B — Admin access to the deployment pipeline.** Pipeline access is a single role: users granted access to a pipeline get pipeline admin rights. Without it the developers cannot open or run the pipeline at all.
- **E — Contributor access to the Development and Test workspaces.** Deploying *into* a stage requires a workspace role that can write items — **Contributor** is the lowest such role, so it satisfies least privilege while still allowing the required deployments.
- **D — Viewer access to the Production workspace.** The developers must be *prevented* from deploying to Production but still need the pipeline to function. **Viewer** is read-only: they can see the Production stage and compare it, but any deployment into it is blocked. Giving them nothing at all would be an option in principle, but Viewer is the level offered and it is read-only.

Rejected:
- **A** *Build permission on the production semantic models* – lets someone build new content on a model; it has nothing to do with deploying and adds privilege without need.
- **C** *Viewer on Development and Test* – read-only, so they could not deploy to the two stages they are supposed to deploy to.
- **F** *Contributor on Production* – would let them deploy to Production, which is the one thing the requirements forbid.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace that contains a DirectQuery semantic model. The model queries a data source that has 500 million rows.
You have a Microsoft Power Bi report named Report1 that uses the model. Report1 contains visuals on multiple pages.
You need to reduce the query execution time for the visuals on all the pages.
What are two features that you can use? Each correct answer presents a complete solution,
NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
Both aggregation features answer a DAX query from a small pre-summarised cache instead of sending it to the 500-million-row source, and both work for **every** visual on **every** page — which is what "all the pages" demands.

- **A — user-defined aggregations.** You build an aggregation table yourself and map its columns to the detail table. The doc: *"Aggregations in Power BI can improve query performance over very large DirectQuery semantic models."* Queries that can be answered from the aggregation hit the cache; only the rest fall through to DirectQuery.
- **B — automatic aggregation.** The same idea, managed for you: Power BI trains on the query log and maintains the aggregation table itself. It is designed specifically for DirectQuery models.

Rejected:
- **C — query caching.** Not available for DirectQuery. The doc's limitation is explicit: query caching applies to models in **Import** mode; it does not apply to DirectQuery or live connections. It also only helps the *initial* page load for returning users, not "all the pages".
- **D — OneLake integration.** A semantic-model setting that writes **Import**-mode table data into OneLake as Delta. It does nothing for a DirectQuery model and is not a query-performance feature.

refs.t: Use aggregations in Power BI Desktop
Query caching in Power BI Premium

B - The AutoAggregations feature automatically creates aggregations on large datasets and based on query optimization determines the total number of rows that requires processing based on the generated query plan. Incorrect to this question context: C - Although caching helps improve performance on large datasets, it doesn't support DirectQuery (Important note in https://learn.microsoft.com/power-bi/connect-data/power-bi-query-caching?wt.mc_id=studentamb_657938) ; Also, it is a feature available in PBI Service that is automatic and needs no intervention from the user.

A. User-defined aggregations (UDAs) allow you to pre-aggregate specific calculations directly in the semantic model. This reduces the amount of data that needs to be retrieved from the source each time a visual requires the calculation, significantly improving query execution time. C. Power BI Desktop enables query caching for DirectQuery models. This stores frequently used queries on the client machine, eliminating the need to re-send them to the source data for subsequent interactions.

Agreed to AB. Both UDA's and AA optimize direct query performance. One just requires more manual work and in depth knowledge data modelling and query optimization techniques (UDA), whereas the other makes simplifies this process through the use of ML algorithms (AA).

User-defined aggregations (A): User-defined aggregations allow you to create pre-aggregated tables that summarize data at a higher level, reducing the volume of data that needs to be queried for specific visuals. This can significantly improve performance for common queries by avoiding the need to scan the entire dataset. Query caching (C): Query caching stores the results of previous queries for reuse. When users interact with visuals that require similar data, the cached results can be returned more quickly than querying the source again, thereby reducing execution time for those visuals.

A. user-defined aggregations Aggregations allow you to precompute summary tables (e.g., sums, averages) at a higher granularity. Power BI can use these instead of querying the full dataset, significantly improving performance. C. query caching Query caching stores the results of previous queries so that repeated queries (such as visuals across multiple pages) can be served quickly without hitting the underlying data source again.
Agreed AB. Although query caching (C) will reduce query execution time too, you risk outdated cached results when working with real-time or dynamic data.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains 30 CSV files in OneLake. The files are updated daily.
You create a Microsoft Power BI semantic model named Model1 that uses the CSV files as a data source. You configure incremental refresh for
Model1 and publish the model to a Premium capacity in the Fabric tenant.
When you initiate a refresh of Model1, the refresh fails after running out of resources.
What is a possible cause of the failure?
questions.explanation:
**Incremental refresh depends on query folding.** The `RangeStart` / `RangeEnd` parameters are supposed to be translated into a filter that the *source* applies, so each partition reads only its own slice. Microsoft states the requirement directly: *"Incremental refresh is designed for data sources that support query folding."* And the failure mode is documented too — when folding does not happen, *"the Power Query engine … must retrieve all rows and then apply the filter locally"*, once **per partition**.

CSV files are flat files: there is no query engine behind them to push a filter into, so nothing folds. Every partition drags in all 30 files in full and filters them in memory, and the refresh runs out of resources. That is exactly **D**.

- **A** – folding *occurring* is the healthy case; it would make the refresh cheap, not fail.
- **B** – *Only refresh complete days* trims the newest partial day. It reduces work slightly; it cannot cause resource exhaustion.
- **C** – the XMLA endpoint governs external-tool connectivity. It has no bearing on a refresh initiated in the service.
- **E** – changing the data type of the partition column breaks incremental refresh with a *schema/type* error, not an out-of-resources failure.

*Note:* 37% of the community picks E, and one highly-voted comment objects that folding "does not make sense on a CSV source". That objection is the answer restated: because a CSV cannot fold, the filters land in memory — which is precisely why the refresh dies.

refs.t: Incremental refresh and real-time data for semantic models

comments.body: D. Query folding is NOT occurring. Query folding refers to the ability of Power Query to push data transformation logic back to the data source, which can perform the transformations more efficiently. When query folding does not occur, all the data is pulled into Power BI and transformations are applied locally, which can be resource-intensive and lead to running out of resources, especially with large datasets like your 30 CSV files. E. The delta type of the column used to partition the data has changed: While this could cause issues with incremental refresh accuracy, it would not typically result in "running out of resources" during the refresh.

For efficient data processing, Power BI aims to push as much of the filtering and calculations as possible to the source system (OneLake in this case). This is called query folding. When query folding fails, Power BI needs to pull all the raw data into the semantic model and perform operations there, increasing memory and processing strain. E This could lead to refresh errors but is less likely to cause the specific behavior of running out of resources.

Correct Option is D) If query folding is not occurring, it means that all 30 CSV files are likely being loaded into memory for processing, which can lead to resource exhaustion, especially if the files are large or numerous. A. Query folding is occurring: If query folding were happening, it would typically improve performance and reduce resource usage, not cause a failure. B. Only refresh complete days is selected: This option usually helps in managing the data being refreshed by only focusing on completed data, potentially alleviating resource issues rather than causing them. C. XMLA Endpoint is set to Read Only: If the XMLA Endpoint were set to read-only, it wouldn't directly cause a refresh failure due to resource issues. It would restrict write operations but not necessarily impact resource allocation during a refresh. E. The delta type of the column used to partition the data has changed: Changes in partitioning columns could cause refresh issues, but they wouldn’t inherently lead to resource exhaustion unless they also disrupt query folding.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a warehouse. The warehouse uses row-level security (RLS).
You create a Direct Lake semantic model that uses the Delta tables and RLS of the warehouse.
When users interact with a report built from the model, which mode will be used by the DAX queries?
questions.explanation:
Direct Lake normally reads Delta/Parquet straight from OneLake with no SQL engine in the path. **Row-level security defined on the warehouse is enforced by the SQL engine**, so a model that must honour warehouse RLS cannot use that shortcut — it has to route the query through SQL. The doc says so in one sentence: *"Power BI queries on a warehouse in Direct Lake mode will fall back to DirectQuery mode to abide by row-level security."*

So the DAX queries run in **DirectQuery** mode — **A**.

- **C Direct Lake** – what the model is *configured* as, but not what the queries end up *using* once RLS forces the fallback. This is the trap, and 43% of the community falls into it.
- **B Dual** – a storage mode you set on a table in a composite model. Direct Lake fallback does not produce it.
- **D Import** – nothing is cached into the model; the data stays in the warehouse.

comments.body: A. Direct Query "Row-level security only applies to queries on a Warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint in Fabric. Power BI queries on a warehouse in Direct Lake mode will fall back to Direct Query mode to abide by row-level security." https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/data-warehouse/row-level-security?wt.mc_id=studentamb_657938

Direct lake . When users interact with a report built from a Direct Lake semantic model that uses Delta tables and RLS of the warehouse, the DAX queries will operate in Direct Lake mode. This mode is specifically designed for analyzing large data volumes in Power BI and is based on loading parquet-formatted files directly from a data lake without querying a Lakehouse or Warehouse endpoint. Unlike DirectQuery, there is no translation from DAX to other query languages, and it does not execute queries on other database systems. This results in performance similar to import mode, with the added benefit of picking up any changes at the data source as they occur12. Direct Lake mode supports row-level security (RLS), ensuring that users only see the data they have permission to view. It combines the advantages of both DirectQuery and import modes while avoiding their disadvantages, making it an ideal choice for very large models and models with frequent updates at the data source2.

Confirm: https://learn.microsoft.com/fabric/get-started/direct-lake-overview?wt.mc_id=studentamb_657938 "Queries using row-level security against tables in the warehouse (including the Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint) will fall back to DirectQuery mode."

The correct answer is A. DirectQuery. When users interact with a report built from a Direct Lake semantic model that uses Delta tables and row-level security (RLS), the DAX queries are executed in DirectQuery mode. This is because RLS requires the queries to be evaluated at the source to enforce security rules dynamically, and Direct Lake does not currently support RLS natively. Therefore, the system falls back to DirectQuery mode to ensure RLS is applied correctly.

Even though created a Direct Lake semantic model, the key detail in this scenario is: RLS is defined at the warehouse level When RLS is enforced at the warehouse (SQL/data source) level, Direct Lake cannot process those security filters inside the in‑memory VertiPaq engine. As a result: The engine cannot stay in Direct Lake mode It must fallback to DirectQuery Therefore, DAX queries are executed in DirectQuery mode

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model. The model uses Direct Lake mode.
You suspect that some DAX queries load unnecessary columns into memory.
You need to identify the frequently used columns that are loaded into memory.
What are two ways to achieve the goal? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
In Direct Lake, columns are **paged into memory on demand** (transcoded from Parquet the first time a query touches them) and stay resident until evicted. To see which columns are actually resident, you need column-segment-level telemetry.

- **C — `$System.DISCOVER_STORAGE_TABLE_COLUMN_SEGMENTS`.** This DMV reports the in-memory segments per column, including the Direct-Lake-specific `TEMPERATURE` and `LAST_ACCESSED` columns. Temperature is literally a frequency-of-use score, so this is the direct answer to "which frequently used columns are loaded into memory".
- **B — VertiPaq Analyzer.** The standard tool (built into DAX Studio and Tabular Editor) that reads those same DMVs and presents per-column size and cardinality. Microsoft's own Direct Lake analysis guidance points at it.

Rejected:
- **A Analyze in Excel** – connects a PivotTable to the model. It tells you nothing about memory residency.
- **D `DISCOVER_MEMORYGRANT`** – reports memory *grants for running queries*, not which columns are paged in.

questions.stem:
You have the source data model shown in the following exhibit.
The primary keys of the tables are indicated by a key symbol beside the columns involved in each key.
You need to create a dimensional data model that will enable the analysis of order items by date, product, and customer.
What should you include in the solution? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
**The ProductID column — Omitted.**

The source is a normalised OLTP model in which `Company` sits beside `Product`, `Customer` and `OrderItem`, and both `Product` and `Customer` carry a **composite primary key** that includes `CompanyID`. The target is a star schema: fact `OrderItem`, dimensions `Date`, `Product`, `Customer`.

**Blank 2 — Omitted.** The stated goal is *"analysis of order items by date, product, and customer"*. `Company` is not one of those dimensions, and in the exhibit the `Company` table has **exactly one column — `CompanyID`**, its own key. A table with no descriptive attributes carries nothing to analyse by and nothing to denormalise; keeping it would only add a join. Dropping it is the correct dimensional-modelling call.

**Blank 1 — The ProductID column.** This follows from blank 2: once `Company` is out of the model, `CompanyID` is no longer part of the key structure, so `OrderItem` relates to `Product` on `ProductID` alone. That is also the only shape a Power BI relationship can take — **model relationships are single-column**; the doc states you *"can't create relationships based on multiple columns"*. That rules out *Both the CompanyID and the ProductID columns* outright, whatever you do with `Company`.

**⚠ This question is genuinely contested — read this before trusting the grade.** Weighted by upvotes the community splits:

| Blank | Reading | Weight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | The ProductID column | **64** |
| 1 | Both CompanyID and ProductID | 32 |
| 1 | A new combined key | 13 |
| 2 | Denormalized into Customer and Product | **84** |
| 2 | Omitted | 25 |

So the community prefers *ProductID* for blank 1 (agreeing with the key) but *Denormalized* for blank 2 (disagreeing with it). Note that the most popular combination, *ProductID + Denormalized*, is **internally inconsistent**: if you denormalise `Company` into `Product` and `Customer`, `CompanyID` survives as an attribute and the product key stays composite — so the relationship could not be on `ProductID` alone. The two self-consistent pairs are **ProductID + Omitted** (the answer key) and **a new combined key + Denormalized**. The key's pair is the one the exam rewards, and the attribute-free `Company` table supports it.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model named Model1. Model1 uses Import mode. Model1 contains a table named Orders.
Orders has 100 million rows and the following fields.
You need to reduce the memory used by Model1 and the time it takes to refresh the model.
Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
Both goals — less memory **and** faster refresh — point at the same two culprits in the table: a very high-cardinality column and a calculated column.

- **A — split `OrderDateTime` into separate date and time columns.** VertiPaq compresses column by column, and compression collapses as cardinality rises. A `Date/Time` down to the second over 100 million rows is close to unique per row — the worst case for the dictionary. Split it and you get at most a few thousand distinct dates and 86,400 distinct times, both of which compress hard. This is Microsoft's own guidance: *"split the column into separate date and time columns"* to reduce model size.
- **D — replace `TotalSalesAmount` with a measure.** It is currently a **calculated column** (`Quantity * Price`). Calculated columns are **materialised at refresh and stored in the model**, so they cost both refresh time and memory — 100 million decimal values of it. A measure is evaluated at query time and stores nothing. The guidance: *"calculated columns … increase the model size and can prolong data refresh time … consider a measure instead."*

Rejected:
- **B — replace `TotalQuantity` with a calculated column.** `TotalQuantity` is already a **measure** (see the Description column). This swaps the cheap thing for the expensive thing — backwards on both goals.
- **C — convert `Quantity` to Text.** Text columns are larger and slower than integers and cannot be aggregated. Strictly worse.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a semantic model.
You need to prevent report creators from populating visuals by using implicit measures.
What are two tools that you can use to achieve the goal? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
NOTE: Each correct answer is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
An *implicit* measure is what Power BI creates on the fly when a report author drags a raw numeric column into a visual and lets it be summarised. You suppress that behaviour with the model-level property **`DiscourageImplicitMeasures`**, which forces authors to use explicit measures instead.

- **A — Power BI Desktop.** Exposed in **Model Explorer** as the semantic model property *Discourage implicit measures* (it is also set automatically the moment you create a calculation group).
- **B — Tabular Editor.** Sets `Model.DiscourageImplicitMeasures` directly against the TOM, which was the only way to do it before Desktop surfaced it.

questions.explanation:
**Some — the Microsoft Power Query engine.**

Read the **step folding indicators** down the Applied steps pane. Power Query marks each step with one of these:

| Indicator | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| *(no icon)* / plain | folds — will be evaluated at the source |
| **orange/red warning icon** | **not folded** — this step breaks folding |
| grey | folding could not be determined |

**Blank 1 — Some.** The early steps (`Source`, `Navigation 1`) fold, but **`Capitalized each word`** carries the not-folded marker. Folding stops at the first step that cannot be translated into the source query, so everything before it folds and everything from it onward does not. That is *some*, not *All* and not *None*.

**Blank 2 — the Microsoft Power Query engine.** `Added custom` sits **after** the break, so it can never be pushed down. The doc: once folding is broken, the remaining transformations *"are processed by the Power Query engine"* — data is pulled out of the source and transformed locally. It is also worth noting this query does an **Appended query** across two different lakehouses; a query that spans two sources has no single engine to fold into, which is why the options naming a lakehouse engine are wrong.

questions.stem:
You have a Fabric tenant that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse’. Lakehouse1 contains a table named Tablet.
You are creating a new data pipeline.
You plan to copy external data to Table’. The schema of the external data changes regularly.
You need the copy operation to meet the following requirements:
Replace Table1 with the schema of the external data.
Replace all the data in Table1 with the rows in the external data.
You add a Copy data activity to the pipeline.
What should you do for the Copy data activity?
questions.explanation:
The Copy data activity's **Destination** tab has a *Table action* setting with two choices, and their documented meanings decide this:

| Table action | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Append** | adds rows to the existing table, keeping its schema |
| **Overwrite** | **drops and recreates the table**, so both the schema and all the data are replaced |

The two requirements — *replace Table1 with the schema of the external data* and *replace all the data* — are exactly what **Overwrite** does, which matters here because *"the schema of the external data changes regularly"*.

- **A** *add additional columns* – appends constant/metadata columns to the source; it does not replace anything.
- **C** *Enable staging* – routes the copy through interim storage for throughput. No effect on schema or on replacing rows.
- **D** *Enable partition discovery* – interprets a folder hierarchy as partition columns when reading.
- **E** *Recursively* – reads sub-folders of the source path.

Note that *truncate*-style behaviour would not be enough even if it were offered: truncating removes rows but leaves the old schema in place.
